blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Recent inversion-free, flow-based image editing methods evolve the source image toward the target via a differential velocity field. We observe that this velocity field does not explicitly account for which regions should be preserved, leading to unintended drift in non-editing regions. To address this, we formulate source fidelity control as a stochastic optimal control problem in which a selective fidelity term on the editing residual is enforced along the editing trajectory. Solving this problem and approximating its solution yields the Residual Gating Principle: each latent component is pulled back toward the source with a gain that decays exponentially with the local residual magnitude, so that small deviations are suppressed while large, semantically meaningful edits pass through unimpeded. The proposed method, RAGE, requires only one lightweight gated interpolation per sampling step, involves no mask estimation, attention maps, retraining, or architecture-specific modifications, and is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors. On PIE-Bench, RAGE achieves the best overall rank among 17 methods and substantially improves background preservation on both Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX backbones while maintaining competitive editing quality.
blocks.zh: 最近的无倒置,以流为主的图像编辑方法通过差速场将源图像向目标进化. 我们注意到,这一速度领域没有明确说明应保留哪些区域,导致非编辑区域意外漂移。 为了解决这个问题,我们制定了源忠贞控制方案,作为一个有条理的最佳控制问题,在编辑轨迹上执行编辑剩余部分的选择性忠贞术语。 解决这一问题并近似其解决办法产生 " 残余物分量原则 " :每个潜在成分被拉回源头,其收益随当地残留量成倍地衰减,从而抑制了小偏差,而大型、精密有意义的编辑则不受阻碍地通过。 拟议的方法RAGE每取样步骤只需要一个轻量级的入门插值,不涉及口罩估计,注意力图,再培训,或特定架构的修改,并被应用在FlowEdit编辑器上. 在PIE-Bench上,RAGE在17个方法中取得了最佳的总体排名,并大大改进了稳定传播3和FLUX主干线上的背景保存,同时保持了竞争性编辑质量.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Recently, inversion-free flow-based image editing
methods ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) have enabled
flexible editing guided by text prompts. They directly solve an
ordinary differential equation (ODE) from a source image to a target
image, without requiring an explicit inversion step. Despite their
different formulations, these methods share a common underlying
structure: the editing process is driven by a differential velocity
field V θ V_{\theta} , which characterizes the difference between the
generative directions conditioned on the target and on the source.

However, flow matching learns transport at the distribution level and
does not explicitly distinguish which regions of a single given source
image should be modified and which should remain unchanged. As a
result, unintended drift occurs in regions unrelated to the edit.
Since each editing step depends on the current state, this drift also
accumulates over the editing trajectory. Even when an edit is
semantically localized, backgrounds may shift, textures may change,
and fine details may be altered (see Fig. 1 ).

Existing methods mitigate this drift from different perspectives.
FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) employs different classifier-free
guidance scales for the source and target and truncates the sampling
timesteps, while other methods rely on attention
injection ( Hertz et al., 2023 ; Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) or explicit mask
estimation ( Couairon et al., 2023 ) .
FlowAlign ( Kim et al., 2026 ) addresses this drift through an
optimal control formulation: it encourages the velocity to remain
close to that of the base editor and imposes a quadratic penalty on
the final editing residual. Here, the editing residual refers
to the deviation of the editing state from the source image.

This terminal penalty encourages the entire final result to remain
close to the source image. In regions that must change to accomplish

blocks.en:
Furthermore, the penalty acts only on the final result, whereas drift
accumulates progressively during the editing process. When drift is
still small, it can be distinguished from intended edits. As it
accumulates, however, this distinction gradually fades, and the drift
becomes increasingly difficult to correct. Yet the terminal penalty
addresses drift only at the end of the editing process. Therefore,
fidelity preservation should be selective and should operate
throughout the editing trajectory, suppressing drift as soon as it
arises.

blocks.en:
To address these challenges, we propose RAGE , a r esidual- a daptive g ating framework for flow-based image e diting that enables selective fidelity preservation throughout the editing trajectory.
We observe that the editing residual of the current state provides a
signal for distinguishing intended edits from unintended drift. The first
modification uses this signal to make fidelity preservation selective.
We replace the quadratic terminal cost with a fidelity term defined on
the editing residual. This term pulls latent components with small
residuals back toward the source image while leaving those with large
residuals unimpeded. The second modification addresses the limitation
of constraining only the final result. We replace the fixed terminal
time with a random terminal time, allowing fidelity preservation to
operate throughout the editing trajectory and thereby yielding a
stochastic optimal control problem.

blocks.en:
Text-guided image editing with pretrained generative models has been
extensively studied. Early diffusion-based approaches manipulate the
internal computation of the denoising network:
Prompt-to-Prompt ( Hertz et al., 2023 ) and
Plug-and-Play ( Tumanyan et al., 2023 ) inject or replace attention

estimates an explicit spatial mask to restrict where edits may
occur. Instruction-based methods such as
InstructPix2Pix ( Brooks et al., 2023 ) finetune the
generative model on paired editing data. A complementary line of work improves the inversion
process itself: Direct Inversion ( Ju et al., 2023 ) corrects the
source branch of inversion-based pipelines with minimal code
changes.

blocks.en: 2.2 Inversion-Based and Inversion-Free Methods
blocks.zh: 2.2 基于颠倒和无颠倒的方法

blocks.en:
With the emergence of flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) as the
backbone of state-of-the-art text-to-image models, editing methods
have been adapted to rectified-flow dynamics. Inversion-based flow
methods first map the source image to a noise representation and
then regenerate under the target prompt:
RF-Inversion ( Rout et al., 2025 ) performs rectified-flow
inversion with dynamic optimal control derived via a linear quadratic
regulator, while RFEdit ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and
FireFlow ( Deng et al., 2025 ) improve the accuracy or efficiency of
reverse-ODE inversion;
FTEdit ( Xu et al., 2025 ) introduces a two-stage inversion with
invariance control for flow transformers; and
DNAEdit ( Xie et al., 2025 ) replaces simulation-based inversion
by directly refining the desired Gaussian noise in the noise domain.
Inversion-free methods bypass the source-to-noise mapping entirely:
FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) constructs a direct ODE between
source and target distributions;
FlowAlign ( Kim et al., 2026 ) adds source-consistency
regularization at the trajectory’s terminal point; and
InfEdit ( Xu et al., 2024 ) performs inversion-free editing with
consistency models. More recently,
SAM-Flow ( Cui et al., 2026 ) restricts the differential velocity
to attention-derived soft masks and anchors the remaining regions
to the source latent, obtaining the masks from an auxiliary
editing pass. Among these methods, FlowAlign is the closest to
ours: it treats source consistency as part of the editing dynamics,
through a terminal penalty in an optimal control formulation.
RAGE keeps this control formulation but replaces the
quadratic terminal penalty with a selective fidelity term on the
editing residual and a random terminal time. Fidelity is thus
enforced along the trajectory, and preservation is gated by the
residual rather than uniform. Because the residual alone decides what
to preserve, RAGE requires no masks or attention maps. It is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors.

therefore act selectively: pull small-residual components back toward

blocks.en: 3.4.4 Instantiations on FlowEdit-Based Editors

blocks.en:
Because the correction ( 15 ) depends only on
the current state and the source latent, it is applied on top of the base editor’s update at each step. We
instantiate RAGE on the inversion-free FlowEdit
framework ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) .
Algorithm 3.4.4 gives the
instantiation used in our FLUX experiments, which follows the
FlowEdit skeleton directly. Algorithm 3.4.4 gives the SD3 instantiation,
which uses the same skeleton and additionally adopts the
source-consistency correction ( 4 ) of FlowAlign ( Kim et al., 2026 ) .
The two algorithms differ only in the base editor: FLUX is a
guidance-distilled model that takes the guidance scale as a model input,
whereas on SD3, classifier-free guidance is applied explicitly to the target
branch.
In both algorithms, RAGE
consists of the steps highlighted in blue, which compute the
gate from the current residual and apply the gated
interpolation ( 15 ), while all remaining lines follow the base editor’s skeleton, with the configuration detailed in Sec. 4.1 . The correction requires no mask estimation, no
attention maps, no retraining, and no architecture-specific
modifications, and it adds negligible overhead (one pointwise
operation per sampling step). To measure this overhead, we run the SD3 instantiation on a subset of 70 images with and without the gate, keeping all other settings fixed. Editing the subset takes 212.907 s with the base editor alone and 214.863 s with RAGE, an increase of 1.956 s in total, or about 0.03 s per image (0.92%).

The main advantage lies in source preservation. The two
instantiations occupy the top two positions on Structure Distance and
on all four background preservation metrics. Compared with
FlowEdit ( Kulikov et al., 2025 ) , the base editor on the same
backbone, RAGE reduces both LPIPS and MSE to about one third

between source preservation and editing strength. Both
instantiations also substantially outperform FlowEdit in Rank Avg.
These improvements come from a single lightweight residual-gated
correction, without mask estimation or attention maps.

Figs. 2 and 3 present twelve
examples from PIE-Bench, one figure for each backbone (FLUX.1-dev and
Stable Diffusion), covering shape modification, object replacement,
color editing, object addition, expression editing, and background
replacement. We compare the results from two perspectives: whether
regions outside the intended edit, including the background, nearby
objects, subject identity, and lighting, remain consistent with the
source image, and whether the requested edit is fully realized. The
former reveals unintended drift, while the latter checks whether
RAGE suppresses this drift while still completing the edit.

(Fig. 3 ), when only the torch should become a

(Fig. 3 , row 6), the “forest” generated by

blocks.en: Residual-gated correction. To evaluate the role of residual-gated correction, we consider the w/o Correction variant, which sets α = 0 \alpha=0 in ( 15 ), leaving only the updates from the base editor. As shown in Table 2 , our full method substantially improves structural and background preservation compared with this variant while maintaining competitive CLIP similarity. These findings suggest that residual-gated correction helps the editor distinguish regions that require modification from those that should remain unchanged, enabling more targeted edits while preserving the surrounding content.

blocks.en: Warm-up. As discussed in Sec. 3.4.3 , the warm-up phase allows sufficient residuals to accumulate before enabling correction, helping distinguish regions that require editing from those that should remain unchanged. To evaluate its contribution, we set K 0 = 0 K_{0}=0 , enabling correction from the first step. We consider two configurations: w/o Warm-up uses the guidance configured for after the warm-up phase throughout all steps, whereas + original schedule retains the original two-stage guidance schedule. As shown in Table 2 , both variants achieve stronger background preservation but lower editing similarity than the full model, indicating that premature correction suppresses intended edits. Their nearly identical results on both backbones suggest that the benefit of the warm-up phase primarily comes from delaying the correction, rather than from the guidance schedule used during this phase.

blocks.en: 4.6 Human Preference Study
blocks.zh: 4.6 人类优先研究

blocks.en:
To complement the automatic metrics, we conduct a human preference
study following the pairwise comparison (2AFC) protocol. We randomly
sample 100 images from PIE-Bench as the source pool. Each
comparison draws one image from this pool, pairs it with a randomly
selected baseline on a randomly assigned backbone (FLUX or SD), and presents the source image, the editing instruction, and two
anonymized outputs (ours and one baseline) in randomized left-right
order. Evaluators are asked to select the output that best balances
editing faithfulness and source preservation, or to indicate “no preference” if both results are comparable. Each evaluator completes
40 comparisons drawn independently from the shared pool. We
collect responses from 15 evaluators, yielding 600 pairwise judgments
(435 decisive, 160 ties, 5 skipped).

blocks.en: 5 Limitations
blocks.zh: 5 限制

blocks.en:
Since the residual gate operates in VAE latent space, RAGE
inherits the reconstruction characteristics, and any
biases, of the pretrained backbone. Extending the residual-gating
mechanism to video editing, pixel-space models, and other generative
paradigms beyond rectified flow is a promising direction for future
work.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We presented RAGE, which makes the velocity field of
flow-based image editing source aware. We formulated fidelity control
as a stochastic optimal control problem, which leads to the Residual
Gating Principle: each latent component is pulled back toward the
source with a gain that decays exponentially as its residual
grows. The resulting algorithm needs only one gated interpolation per
sampling step, with no masks, attention maps, retraining, or
architectural changes, and is applied on top of FlowEdit-based editors.
On PIE-Bench, RAGE achieves the best overall rank among 17
methods and delivers large, consistent gains in background
preservation over its base editor on both SD3 and FLUX backbones
while maintaining competitive editing quality. We believe the broader
idea of deriving source-aware generative dynamics from optimal control
with selective residual fidelity extends beyond image editing, and we
hope it motivates source-aware formulations in video editing, 3D
editing, and other conditional generation tasks.
